slides.heading: Sunset Views
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Stacks
slides.narration: Let's solve Sunset Views, a medium stacks problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Buildings face EAST or WEST; return ascending indices of buildings that can see the sunset (strictly taller than everything in front of them in that direction).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Buildings face EAST or WEST; return ascending indices of buildings that can see the sunset (strictly taller than everything in front of them in that direction).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: A building sees the sunset if it's taller than everything between it and the sun.
slides.narration: A building sees the sunset if it's taller than everything between it and the sun.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: For each building check all ahead → O(n²)
Scan from the sunset side tracking the max → O(n)
Or a stack scanning the other way
slides.narration: Checking every building against all the ones in front is quadratic. Scanning from the sunset side and tracking the tallest seen so far is linear.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 3. Buildings taller than the max can see
slides.narration: Step by step. First, scan from the sunset side. Second, keep the running max. Third, buildings taller than the max can see. Fourth, return indices in order.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We scan from the sunset side, adding an index whenever its height beats the running max, then reverse the list when facing east.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is O of n.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
slides.narration: Equal height blocks the view. Return the indices in ascending order, so reverse when scanning east.

bullets: A building sees the sunset if it's taller than everything between it and the sun.
